Slides (black), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from the lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no vascular chapter. Mesenteric ischaemia and vascular trauma aren't on this year's slides but are asked often — they are at the end with added background.

  • Three emergencies, one logic: identify the arterial pathology, act before tissue is lost, and anticipate what happens after flow is restored.

1. Acute limb ischaemia (ALI)

  • ALI = a sudden decrease in limb perfusion causing a potential threat to limb viability — acute arterial occlusion.

Pathophysiology

  • Nerves: most sensitive to ischaemia. Skin and bone: relatively resistant. Muscle: the major structural component — local and systemic manifestations of ischaemia–reperfusion injury.
TissueCritical ischaemic time
Muscle4 h
Nerve8 h
Fat13 h
Skin24 h
Bone4 days

History & examination

  • Leg symptoms relate to pain or function: duration and intensity of pain, presence of motor or sensory changes. Previous PVD (claudication), aneurysm, heart disease, atherosclerotic risk factors.
  • The 6 Ps: pain · pallor · pulselessness · paraesthesia · paralysis · poikilothermia.

Acute ischaemia — pale foot compared with the normal side

  • Early: pain, pallor, pulselessness, cold. Sensory loss before motor — paralysis is late and means advanced, possibly irreversible ischaemia.
  • Classic vignette: woman with AF who stopped warfarin for a dental procedure → 2 h of sudden severe leg pain → embolic ALI.
  • Most concerning symptom in acute limb ischaemia → paraesthesia (nerve ischaemia = threatened limb). 435
  • Presentation of acute critical limb ischaemia among the options → paralysis. 438

Investigations

  • Basic labs · Doppler US · duplex US · CTA · MRA · angiography — "Do we really need investigations?"
  • Site of occlusion: peripheral pulse – area of pain – area of ischaemia.
  • Pulses localize: femoral present, distal absent → femoropopliteal; one femoral absent → ipsilateral iliac; both absent → aortic bifurcation (saddle).
  • Classic embolic ALI: don't delay for imaging — exam and pulses localize; CTA only if it won't delay. Acute-on-chronic: imaging usually needed to plan angioplasty/bypass.

Aetiology

  • Arterial embolism · acute arterial thrombosis · arterial injury · acute arterial dissection.
  • Arterial embolism: occlusion of a previously unobstructed vessel → the most severe ischaemia. Suspect with acute onset, no previous claudication, a risk of embolism, unilateral abnormal findings.
Source of emboliShare
Cardiogenic — atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, other80%
Non-cardiac — aneurysmal disease, proximal atheroma, paradoxical emboli10%
Other/idiopathic10%
  • Arteriographic signs of embolism: meniscus sign · lack of collaterals · absence of atherosclerosis.

Angiogram — abrupt cut-off with a meniscus sign; retrieved embolus

Common sites where emboli lodge (bifurcations — femoral, popliteal); embolus blocking the artery

  • Acute arterial thrombosis: usually in vessels with pre-existing atherosclerosis; ischaemia often less severe than with embolism; the location of occlusion affects severity.

Atherosclerotic narrowing — sites of thrombosis

ThrombosisEmbolism
Previous claudicationNo previous symptoms of arterial insufficiency
No source of emboliObvious source (AF, MI)
Long history (days to weeks)Sudden onset (hours to days)
Less severe ischaemiaSevere ischaemia
Lack of pulses in the contralateral legNormal pulses in the contralateral leg
Positive signs of chronic ischaemiaNo signs of chronic ischaemia

Angiograms — acute embolism (sharp cut-off, no collaterals) vs acute thrombosis (diffuse disease, collaterals)

  • Acute-on-chronic ischaemia can look deceptively mild — collaterals keep some supply; the full 6 Ps may be absent. Thrombosis is also iatrogenic (femoral sheath after catheterization) or traumatic (knee dislocation → popliteal intimal tear).
  • Most common cause of acute lower-limb ischaemia → embolization from the heart. 435 ×2

Severity

  • Reversible — mild: pain, pallor, poikilothermia · moderate: paraesthesia, paresis · severe: analgesia, paralysis, muscle tenderness.
  • Irreversible: fixed skin staining, muscle rigor.

2. Management of ALI

  • Systemic anticoagulation + revascularization (surgical; endovascular: thrombolysis, percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy).
  • Anticoagulation goals: decrease thrombus propagation and prevent recurrent embolization. Unfractionated heparin: bolus 80 U/kg, infusion 18 U/kg/h. Immediately after diagnosis (take blood samples first); hold only if early angiography is available.
  • Revascularization: surgical embolectomy · endovascular — catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT), percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy.
  • Acute limb ischaemia → IV heparin + revascularization. 437 ×2
  • AF after an MI, sudden pale painful right leg, femoral pulse present, absent below, normal left leg → urgent embolectomy. 439 ×2

Surgical embolectomy

  • Ideal treatment for arterial embolism: rapid diagnosis, identified source, rapid systemic anticoagulation, surgical embolectomy. Timely operation is the goal — pre-op preparation should be minimal.
  • Groin incision landmark: midpoint between the pubic symphysis and the ASIS.

Groin incision over the common femoral artery and the femoral anatomy

Expose and control the common, superficial and deep femoral arteries; femoral arteriotomy (transverse, longitudinal, oblique)

Fogarty balloon embolectomy catheter — blind passage proximally and distally (or over-the-wire under fluoroscopy), proper sizing, inflate and withdraw

Technical goals — forceful pulsatile inflow and back-bleeding

  • Fogarty steps: expose the CFA → arteriotomy → pass the deflated balloon beyond the clot → inflate → withdraw with the clot → restore flow and close.

Thrombolysis

  • No role for systemic thrombolysis. Catheter-directed thrombolysis: less invasive, reduced mortality — initial treatment of choice for class I and IIa ischaemia.
  • Agents: streptokinase · urokinase · tPA.
  • Percutaneous mechanical/aspiration thrombectomy — combined with CDT speeds clot lysis and reduces the thrombolytic dose.
  • CDT: catheter into the thrombus, local tPA for ~12 h, then repeat angiography — less bleeding than systemic lysis; for patients unfit for surgery or acute-on-chronic disease.

Amputation

  • Major amputation in up to 25%: 10% irreversible ischaemia; 10–15% after revascularization.

3. Complications of ALI

  • Ischaemia–reperfusion syndrome · compartment syndrome · rhabdomyolysis.
  • Ischaemia–reperfusion triad: hyperkalaemia · metabolic acidosis · myoglobinuria.
  • Compartment syndrome: ↑ capillary permeability → local oedema → compartment hypertension. Pain out of proportion, paraesthesia, oedema. Compartment pressure > 25 mmHg = clear indication for fasciotomy.

The four leg compartments (anterior, lateral, superficial and deep posterior) — two-incision fasciotomy

  • Rhabdomyolysis: tubular necrosis from myoglobin precipitation → tea-coloured urine, raised creatinine → hydration, alkalinizing the urine.
  • Pulses don't exclude compartment syndrome — the microcirculation fails while arterial pressure (100–130) exceeds compartment pressure (25–40). Prophylactic fasciotomy after prolonged ischaemia.
  • Before releasing the clamps, warn anaesthesia — K⁺ washout (treat with insulin–glucose, salbutamol) and lactic acidosis (bicarbonate) → arrhythmias. Myoglobin → AKI → IV fluids, watch urine colour and output.
  • After revascularization of a traumatic ischaemic leg — the reperfusion complication → hyperkalaemia. 436

4. Aneurysms

  • Aneurysm = > 50% increase in diameter compared with the adjacent normal segment (× 1.5). Normal infrarenal aorta: men 2–2.4 cm, women 1.6–2.2 cm. Infrarenal aorta > 3 cm = AAA.
  • Distribution: aorta 90–95%; peripheral — popliteal, femoral; visceral — splenic. AAA > 3 cm prevalence 5–8.4% (women 1.5%); a disease of Western nations, rare in Asian populations.
  • True aneurysm: involves all three layers. False aneurysm: disruption of the wall with blood outside the normal layers — the wall is compressed surrounding tissue.

True aneurysm (normal vs aneurysmal aorta) · false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) on angiography

  • Aetiology: degenerative (most common — calcification, atherosclerosis, matrix metalloproteinases, genetic + environmental) · post-dissection · inflammatory (Takayasu, giant-cell arteritis, Behçet's) · traumatic (false) · infection (primary/secondary) · congenital (tuberous sclerosis, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, coarctation).
  • Risk factors: age ≥ 65 · male (M:F 4:1) · white race · family history · smoking · HTN · hyperlipidaemia · PAD & CAD.
  • Exam trap: diabetes is NOT an AAA risk factor — it is inversely (protectively) associated. 1.0 → 1.3 cm is ectasia; ≥ 1.5 × normal is an aneurysm.

Natural history & rupture risk

  • Gradual or sporadic expansion, 0.3–0.5 cm/year. Complications: rupture, thromboembolism, compression.
AAA diameterAnnual rupture risk
< 5 cm< 5%
5–6 cm10%
6–7 cm15–20%
> 7 cm70%

Presentation & detection

  • Asymptomatic (incidental) · symptomatic (abdominal/back pain from leak or rapid expansion; compression) · rupture — 35% present this way: abdominal/back pain + hypotension + pulsatile mass.
  • Physical examination is not sensitive — 48% diagnosed clinically; exam missed 38% of radiological cases.
  • Ultrasound: highly sensitive and specific — screening, diagnosis and monitoring.
  • CT: sensitive and specific — pre-operative assessment.
  • Angiogram: not reliable — false negative (normal lumen because of thrombus).

Pulsatile abdominal mass · ultrasound of an AAA

CT of an AAA with mural thrombus · angiogram showing only the lumen

Indications for surgery — rupture risk > surgical risk

  • Size > 5 cm in women, > 5.5 cm in men · symptomatic · ruptured · rapid expansion > 5 mm in 6 months.
  • Options: open surgery with graft replacement · EVAR. Mortality: elective open 5%, EVAR 1%.

Open repair with a sewn-in graft · endovascular stent-graft (EVAR)

  • Ruptured AAA: 100% mortality untreated; OR mortality 50%. Clinical diagnosis — sudden back pain + shock + pulsatile mass. US in the emergency, CT if stable · ABC, crossmatch · emergency repair.
  • Symptomatic AAA → admit, urgent repair within 2–3 days, no size threshold. (Full aneurysm details are in the Aneurysms lecture.)
  • Pulsatile mass behind the knee (popliteal aneurysm) — the most significant complication → thrombosis and distal embolization (rupture is rare). 442 ×2

5. Carotid artery disease

  • Atherosclerosis of the internal carotid artery → stenosis, reduced brain supply and showering of small atherosclerotic debris.
  • Risk factors — non-modifiable: age, male, after menopause, family history, genetic abnormalities. Modifiable major: smoking, HTN, DM, hypercholesterolaemia. Minor: sedentary life, obesity, stress, type A personality, high carbohydrate intake, ↑ homocysteine.
  • Presentation: asymptomatic · symptomatic — amaurosis fugax, TIA, stroke.
  • Investigations: non-invasive carotid duplex · minimally invasive CTA, MRI/MRA · invasive carotid angiogram.
  • Management (symptomatic): < 50–60% stenosis → risk-factor modification + best medical treatment; 60–70% and above → carotid endarterectomy or carotid stenting.
  • CEA complications: stroke · cranial-nerve injury · bleeding/haematoma · restenosis · infection.
  • Events come from artery-to-artery microembolization of soft plaque, not low flow (2 carotids + 2 vertebrals give collaterals). Plaque at the bifurcation/proximal ICA; the ICA has no neck branches, the ECA does.
  • Laterality: limb deficit = contralateral; amaurosis fugax = ipsilateral ("eye same side, body opposite"). TIA resolves within 24 h.
  • Notes' rule: symptomatic > 50% → CEA; complete ICA occlusion → no CEA (nothing left to embolize). CEA hypoglossal injury → tongue deviates to the operated side; neck haematoma can threaten the airway.
Threshold for intervention in symptomatic stenosis: the slide says 60–70% and above; the notes say > 50%. Trials (NASCET) show the largest benefit at ≥ 70% and a smaller benefit at 50–69%. Either way, a symptomatic 80% stenosis → endarterectomy.
  • Transient right-hand weakness for 1 hour + 80% left ICA stenosis → presentation = transient ischaemic attack. 439 ×6
  • A carotid bruit is heard → keyed auscultate the precordium (a radiating aortic-stenosis murmur can mimic a carotid bruit); a true bruit is then assessed with carotid duplex. 427 ×2

6. Mesenteric ischaemia (past papers)

Added explanationAcute mesenteric ischaemia: embolic (AF, recent MI — the commonest, lodges in the SMA just beyond the middle colic origin) · thrombotic (on atherosclerosis; history of postprandial pain) · non-occlusive (NOMI) — low-flow states: septic/cardiogenic shock, vasopressors, digoxin · mesenteric venous thrombosis. Pain out of proportion to examination, then peritonitis; ↑ WBC and lactate. CT angiography is the investigation of choice. Treatment: resuscitation, heparin, laparotomy (embolectomy/revascularization + resection of dead bowel, second look); NOMI → treat the cause, intra-arterial vasodilators (papaverine).
Added explanationSMA territory: jejunum, ileum, caecum, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. Chronic mesenteric ischaemia ("intestinal angina"): postprandial abdominal pain + food fear + weight loss. Ischaemic colitis: elderly, LLQ pain and bloody diarrhoea, watershed areas (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid).
  • Elderly woman with AF, severe abdominal pain, WBC 24, lactate 8 → bowel (mesenteric) ischaemia. 442 ×24
  • ICU patient in septic shock develops abdominal pain, distension and lactic acidosis → non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia. 442 ×2
  • AF + IHD with acute abdominal pain → most likely to reveal the diagnosis → CT scan abdomen (CT angiography). 430
  • SMA thrombosis → ischaemia of the small intestine, caecum and ascending colon; ischaemia of jejunum, ileum and caecum → SMA. 438 ×4 439
  • Chronic mesenteric ischaemia → postprandial pain and weight loss. 437
  • 80-year-old with AF on digoxin, 16 h of severe pain, distension, guarding, WBC 28, bowel-wall oedema → surgical exploration (fixed — the source keys conflicted: antibiotics vs heparin). 435 ×3
  • Diabetic 72-year-old, LLQ pain + bloody diarrhoea, fever → ischaemic colitis. 434 ×4

7. Vascular trauma & iatrogenic injury (past papers)

Added explanationHard signs of arterial injury → immediate surgical exploration: pulsatile bleeding, expanding/pulsatile haematoma, absent distal pulses, palpable thrill/audible bruit, signs of distal ischaemia. Soft signs (non-expanding haematoma, diminished pulse, adjacent nerve injury, proximity) → imaging (CT angiography) or ABI first.
  • Hard sign of vascular injury → active pulsatile bleeding / expanding haematoma. 442
  • Gunshot to the arm — the finding suggesting arterial injury needing urgent angiography/surgery → diminished distal pulses. 432 ×3
  • Stable penetrating thigh wound, non-expanding haematoma, weak but palpable pulses (soft signs) → CT angiography. 442
  • Local complication of angiography/angioplasty → pseudoaneurysm (at the puncture site). 438

Mastery checklist (notes)

  • Embolism hits a normal artery with no collaterals → sudden, severe; acute-on-chronic has collaterals → milder.
  • 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, cold early; paraesthesia before paralysis; paralysis = advanced.
  • Pulses localize the occlusion (femoral present → femoropopliteal; one absent → iliac; both → bifurcation).
  • Embolic ALI → IV heparin + urgent revascularization, no imaging delay.
  • Fogarty embolectomy via the CFA vs catheter-directed thrombolysis.
  • Compartment pressure > 25 mmHg; pulses don't exclude it → fasciotomy.
  • Reperfusion: K⁺, acidosis (warn anaesthesia), myoglobin → AKI (IV fluids).
  • Aneurysm ≥ 1.5 × normal; infrarenal most common; diabetes protective; repair ≥ 5.5 cm men.
  • Carotid: microemboli; limb deficit contralateral, amaurosis ipsilateral; duplex; symptomatic > 50% → CEA; occluded → no CEA.
